title: How to ship a database every day
excerpt: We deploy many database upgrades every day across ~100 public, single-tenant, and BYOC clusters. It would be insane to use Terraform or Helm to do that, so we built our own control plane.
content_html:
August 14, 2026•Tarun Pothulapati (Engineer)

Every day, turbopuffer customers ask for things: new query plans, new APIs, new index structures. In response, we deploy dozens of database upgrades per day across our clusters, many of them the same day we open the PR. Shipping fast is how we make every customer feel like they're our only customer.

We don't want to limit where you can run turbopuffer, so we support many regions across three deployment models: public SaaS, single-tenant SaaS, and BYOC. In total, we operate 100+ clusters, twice as many as we had 6 months ago, and growing as we add more public regions and many more BYOC deployments.

The problem with BYOC

BYOC clusters live inside our customers' cloud accounts, to which we hold no credentials by default. We can't just SSH or kubectl in. Some BYOC vendors solve this by asking the customer to carve out a dedicated cloud account and grant the vendor standing admin credentials inside it. That keeps the rest of the customer's cloud account isolated, but every dedicated account creates security monitoring + compliance + billing overhead that we generally prefer to avoid.

We don't want different control planes for BYOC and SaaS, so we have to design for the lowest common denominator. We must be able to operate every cluster without reaching in.

How do you operate a database cluster you can't touch?

The only way this works is if every operation we need to perform on a cluster can run without us reaching in. The cluster must be able to independently drive its operations to a terminal state, even if it loses its connection to the central control plane.

The solution to this is standard Kubernetes stuff. On every cluster, we run a local cluster agent that implements a simple state machine. A single Kubernetes CRD called TurbopufferOperation expresses every operation kind, from upgrade to tidy. A Kubernetes controller drives each custom resource (CR) from state to state via a reconciliation loop until it reaches a terminal state. Operations advance on their own by default, but BYOC customers can gate operations on approval or maintenance windows. These are baked into the CRD as waiting states that advance when approvals are given or the window opens.

The key is to define states that are generic enough to model every operation kind, both existing and future, but finite enough that the reconciler can always drive them toward a terminal state. We never need to reach in to do work, and the state lives as a durable object in the cluster's own etcd. If the agent crashes or loses its connection to the control plane, it can still drive that work to completion.

The local, durable state machine means we don't have to reach into a cluster to drive its work, but how does a cluster get its work?

You use Terraform, right?

The default here would be to reach for infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tools like Terraform and Helm. These tools are great for provisioning infrastructure. We use them for that! But they're the wrong control plane for operating a fleet of databases.

First, we do not have a dedicated DevOps function at turbopuffer. We ask our database engineers to deploy their code to the infra. Most of them haven't used IaC tools much in the past, so it doesn't make sense to put those tools in their critical path.

Second, Terraform's default model would require us to run terraform apply from our own infrastructure with the customer's infra as the target, which we can't do for BYOC. A GitOps flow for Terraform could solve this by having the customer automatically trigger terraform apply from within their cloud account whenever a Git repo is updated. For database upgrades, this could theoretically work: just bump the Docker image in the Terraform config. But who owns the repo? If it's ours, BYOC customers who want an approval gate have no control over merges. If it's theirs, we're back to needing write access into their systems or waiting on humans to merge the PR.

Either way, many of our operations have a less declarative shape. Things like one-off namespace reindexing, compacting a WAL, or garbage collecting the LSM are jobs to be done, not states to be arrived at. Every ad hoc operation would need to be a git commit with a new manifest to create the job, then a commit to garbage collect the completed jobs. Terraform files make great declarative manifests, but terrible job queues.

How the agent fetches work (and how we keep track of it)

We can't reach into a cluster, and we won't use GitOps, but the cluster still needs to be able to pull its work from the control plane and push its status back out. The system must be fully tolerant of a lost connection between cluster and control plane; a control plane outage should not take down an otherwise healthy cluster. In the event of a lost connection, the cluster should be able to pick up its new operations once it reconnects, while the control plane should be able to catch up on the state of the cluster.

To accomplish these aims, we built a custom central control plane consisting of an API server backed by a PlanetScale MySQL database.

Each cluster agent is given a cluster-specific API key. To fetch its operations, the agent regularly polls the API server via an authenticated GET request, to which the API server responds with that cluster's pending operations. Once the agent gets its operations, it stores them as custom resources and starts running them through its reconciliation loop. This is idempotent: each operation's CR is named with that operation's ID, so if for some reason a later GET returns the same operation again, the agent will just find the existing CR and resume from the state stored in etcd instead of creating a duplicate.

As the operations advance, the cluster agent will periodically POST its buffered status transitions back to the API server, which mirrors them into a status_transitions table in MySQL as an append-only log.

If the agent's POST fails to get a response, the agent puts the transitions back into its buffer and tries again. The POST may have landed even if the response didn't come back, so the same transition could show up twice in the log. That doesn't matter: an operation's current state is just its latest transition.

This is how we keep the central control plane in sync with each cluster even in the event of temporary connection loss. The database maintains the source of truth for the desired operations we want to run on every cluster, and holds a mirror of the status of those operations so we can rebuild a cluster's state from afar.

But a database is a dangerous interface. We said we didn't want to ship code with YAML — it would be insane to replace that with INSERT INTO SQL statements.

An interface we actually like using

We deploy every day, multiple times per day, and debug and maintain the clusters in between deploys. If you're a turbopuffer database engineer, you want the control plane to be as reliable and easy to use as your favorite code editor.

The control plane has a custom Remix/React dashboard that fronts the API server. The UX is inspired by Linear: everything has a hotkey, so you can operate it entirely from the keyboard. The information hierarchy is structured, and the selection state is clear, so you know exactly which clusters you're working on.

Upgrades are the most common operation, and the UI reflects that. We can quickly see each cluster's deployed commit SHA and how far it has drifted from the latest passing SHA, with metadata pulled from GitHub (commit message, PR number, commit date) so we don't have to decipher the SHA. Upgrades are typically done in groups, so we can select multiple clusters across all deployment models, choose a target commit SHA, and upgrade all of them from the keyboard. We can similarly kick off all other operations from this UI.

We don't expect our engineers to be in the dashboard all the time, so we stream status transitions for each operation into a dedicated Slack thread. If an operation fails, it fails loudly into the channel for people to react to and fix. This gets our attention without us having to babysit.

When an approval is needed for operations on a BYOC cluster, the same Slack integration automatically notifies the customer through their dedicated Slack support channel so they can approve.

The control plane also provides a convenient jumping-off point for all the debugging and monitoring interfaces we use. If we want to watch an operation closely, we can jump from the control plane directly into Datadog logs, traces, or metrics scoped to its cluster(s). When a customer reports high latency, we can quickly pull up the memory/CPU profile in Polar Signals for their query pods. When a customer wants a limit bumped for a namespace, we can inspect the namespace and update the config right there (really!). When all the tools you need are right at hand, you feel more connected to your infra, and on-call sucks a lot less.

This dashboard is not just a vibe-coded sidecar to the control plane. We treat it as first-class software and invest engineering effort into it, so the complexity of operating the clusters stays mostly hidden behind a simple, fast, keyboard-driven interface.

Fleet operations

While the control plane has scaled very well, we started to feel the toil of fleet-wide upgrades: manually selecting clusters and a target SHA, kicking off the upgrade, monitoring it, and making sure things looked ok before proceeding to the rest. The larger our fleet got, the more painful it became to sequence and babysit a rollout that could last hours.

Now, any operation can be submitted as a fleet operation, and the control plane's fleet controller will roll it out across a sequence of waves containing one or more clusters. Between waves, a gate checks that every cluster in the wave upgraded successfully and that our monitors are quiet. If a monitor fires or any cluster fails, the fleet controller pauses the rollout and notifies us in Slack, limiting the fallout from a bad deploy.

Importantly, nothing changes for the cluster agent. It has no concept of a fleet or fleet operation. It still polls the API server for its pending operations, and its status transitions are still mirrored back into the same MySQL table. Every operation is still the same CRD driven by the same local state machine. Orchestrating 100s of them is effectively just a loop over existing primitives.

Simplicity scales

turbopuffer's architecture is easy to reason about and easy to be on call for. It would be a shame if it wasn't also easy to deploy to. The design decisions we make in the control plane all funnel toward simplicity: a single control plane for all deployment models, a single CRD for every operation, a single UI to manage the entire fleet.

This simplicity has allowed us to scale the control plane from managing just a few public regions to 100+ clusters across dozens of regions and multiple deployment models. We believe its simplicity will allow us to maintain our shipping speed even as we scale to 1000s.

turbopuffer

turbopuffer is a fast search engine that hosts 1T+ documents, handles 10M+ writes/s, and serves 25k+ queries/s. We are ready for far more. We hope you'll trust us with your queries.

We can't just SSH or kubectl in. Some BYOC vendors solve this by asking the customer to carve out a dedicated cloud account and grant the vendor standing admin credentials inside it. That keeps the rest of the customer's cloud account isolated, but every dedicated account creates security monitoring + compliance + billing overhead that we generally prefer to avoid. We don't want different control planes for BYOC and SaaS, so we have to design for the lowest common denominator. We must be able to operate every cluster without reaching in. How do you operate a database cluster you can't touch? The only way this works is if every operation we need to perform on a cluster can run without us reaching in. The cluster must be able to independently drive its operations to a terminal state, even if it loses its connection to the central control plane. The solution to this is standard Kubernetes stuff. On every cluster, we run a local cluster agent that implements a simple state machine. A single Kubernetes CRD called TurbopufferOperation expresses every operation kind, from upgrade to tidy. A Kubernetes controller drives each custom resource (CR) from state to state via a reconciliation loop until it reaches a terminal state. Operations advance on their own by default, but BYOC customers can gate operations on approval or maintenance windows. These are baked into the CRD as waiting states that advance when approvals are given or the window opens. ╔═ operation lifecycle ═══════════════════════════════════════════╗ ║ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ REQUIRES_APPROVAL ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ │ approve (auto or manual) ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ PENDING ┃ ──▶ ┃ AWAITING_MAINTENANCE_WINDOW ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━┛ ◀── ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ │ start() ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ RUNNING ┃ ──▶ ┃ AWAITING_EXTERNAL_EXECUTION ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━┛ ◀── ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ │ poll() ║░ ║ ┌────┴────┐ ║░ ║ ▼ ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━┓ ┏━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃SUCCESS┃ ┃FAILURE┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━┛ ┗━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ║░ ╚═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝░ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░╔═ operation lifecycle ════╗ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ REQUIRES_APPROVAL ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ▼ approve ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ PENDING ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ▼ start() ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ RUNNING ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ▼ poll() ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━┓ ┏━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ SUCCESS ┃ ┃ FAILURE ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━┛ ┗━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ╚══════════════════════════╝░ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ The key is to define states that are generic enough to model every operation kind, both existing and future, but finite enough that the reconciler can always drive them toward a terminal state. We never need to reach in to do work, and the state lives as a durable object in the cluster's own etcd. If the agent crashes or loses its connection to the control plane, it can still drive that work to completion. The local, durable state machine means we don't have to reach into a cluster to drive its work, but how does a cluster get its work? You use Terraform, right? The default here would be to reach for infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tools like Terraform and Helm. These tools are great for provisioning infrastructure. We use them for that! But they're the wrong control plane for operating a fleet of databases. First, we do not have a dedicated DevOps function at turbopuffer. We ask our database engineers to deploy their code to the infra. Most of them haven't used IaC tools much in the past, so it doesn't make sense to put those tools in their critical path. Second, Terraform's default model would require us to run terraform apply from our own infrastructure with the customer's infra as the target, which we can't do for BYOC. A GitOps flow for Terraform could solve this by having the customer automatically trigger terraform apply from within their cloud account whenever a Git repo is updated. For database upgrades, this could theoretically work: just bump the Docker image in the Terraform config. But who owns the repo? If it's ours, BYOC customers who want an approval gate have no control over merges. If it's theirs, we're back to needing write access into their systems or waiting on humans to merge the PR. Either way, many of our operations have a less declarative shape. Things like one-off namespace reindexing, compacting a WAL, or garbage collecting the LSM are jobs to be done, not states to be arrived at. Every ad hoc operation would need to be a git commit with a new manifest to create the job, then a commit to garbage collect the completed jobs. Terraform files make great declarative manifests, but terrible job queues. How the agent fetches work (and how we keep track of it) We can't reach into a cluster, and we won't use GitOps, but the cluster still needs to be able to pull its work from the control plane and push its status back out. The system must be fully tolerant of a lost connection between cluster and control plane; a control plane outage should not take down an otherwise healthy cluster. In the event of a lost connection, the cluster should be able to pick up its new operations once it reconnects, while the control plane should be able to catch up on the state of the cluster. To accomplish these aims, we built a custom central control plane consisting of an API server backed by a PlanetScale MySQL database. Each cluster agent is given a cluster-specific API key. To fetch its operations, the agent regularly polls the API server via an authenticated GET request, to which the API server responds with that cluster's pending operations. Once the agent gets its operations, it stores them as custom resources and starts running them through its reconciliation loop. This is idempotent: each operation's CR is named with that operation's ID, so if for some reason a later GET returns the same operation again, the agent will just find the existing CR and resume from the state stored in etcd instead of creating a duplicate. As the operations advance, the cluster agent will periodically POST its buffered status transitions back to the API server, which mirrors them into a status_transitions table in MySQL as an append-only log. tpuf engineers │ ▼ ╔═ control plane ═══════╗ ╔═ cluster ══════════════════╗ ║ ║░ ║ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┏━ cluster agent ━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ UI ┃ ║░ ║ ┃┌──────────────────────┐┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ┃│ k8s controller │┃ ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┃│ (sync + reconciler) │┃ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║◀─── GET operations ───║ ┃└───────────┬──────────┘┃ ║░ ║ ┃ API server ┃ ║░ ║ ┃ ▼ ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━┛ ║◀── POST transitions ──║ ┃┌──────────────────────┐┃ ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┃│ TurbopufferOperation │┃ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃│ CRs │┃ ║░ ║ ┃MySQL (PlanetScale)┃ ║░ ║ ┃└──────────────────────┘┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ║░ ║ ║░ ╚═══════════════════════╝░ ╚════════════════════════════╝░ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ tpuf engineers │ ▼ ╔═ control plane ════════════╗ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ UI ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ API server ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━┯━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ║ ▼ ║░ ║ ┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃ MySQL ┃ ║░ ║ ┃ (PlanetScale) ┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ╚════════════════════════════╝░ ░░░░░▲░░░░░░░░░░░▲░░░░░░░░░░░░ │GET work │POST state │ │ ╔═ cluster ══════════════════╗ ║ ┏━ cluster agent ━━━━━━━━┓ ║░ ║ ┃┌──────────────────────┐┃ ║░ ║ ┃│ k8s controller │┃ ║░ ║ ┃│ (sync + reconciler) │┃ ║░ ║ ┃└───────────┬──────────┘┃ ║░ ║ ┃ ▼ ┃ ║░ ║ ┃┌──────────────────────┐┃ ║░ ║ ┃│ TurbopufferOperation │┃ ║░ ║ ┃│ CRs │┃ ║░ ║ ┃└──────────────────────┘┃ ║░ ║ ┗━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┛ ║░ ╚════════════════════════════╝░ ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ If the agent's POST fails to get a response, the agent puts the transitions back into its buffer and tries again. The POST may have landed even if the response didn't come back, so the same transition could show up twice in the log. That doesn't matter: an operation's current state is just its latest transition. This is how we keep the central control plane in sync with each cluster even in the event of temporary connection loss. The database maintains the source of truth for the desired operations we want to run on every cluster, and holds a mirror of the status of those operations so we can rebuild a cluster's state from afar. But a database is a dangerous interface. We said we didn't want to ship code with YAML — it would be insane to replace that with INSERT INTO SQL statements. An interface we actually like using We deploy every day, multiple times per day, and debug and maintain the clusters in between deploys. If you're a turbopuffer database engineer, you want the control plane to be as reliable and easy to use as your favorite code editor. The control plane has a custom Remix/React dashboard that fronts the API server. The UX is inspired by Linear: everything has a hotkey, so you can operate it entirely from the keyboard. The information hierarchy is structured, and the selection state is clear, so you know exactly which clusters you're working on. Upgrades are the most common operation, and the UI reflects that. We can quickly see each cluster's deployed commit SHA and how far it has drifted from the latest passing SHA, with metadata pulled from GitHub (commit message, PR number, commit date) so we don't have to decipher the SHA. Upgrades are typically done in groups, so we can select multiple clusters across all deployment models, choose a target commit SHA, and upgrade all of them from the keyboard. We can similarly kick off all other operations from this UI. Your browser does not support the video tag.0:00 / 0:00Select clusters, pick a target SHA, and roll out upgrades from the keyboard. We don't expect our engineers to be in the dashboard all the time, so we stream status transitions for each operation into a dedicated Slack thread. If an operation fails, it fails loudly into the channel for people to react to and fix. This gets our attention without us having to babysit. When an approval is needed for operations on a BYOC cluster, the same Slack integration automatically notifies the customer through their dedicated Slack support channel so they can approve. 01 / 02Upgrade threads show commit diffs, rollout status, and the conversation around the operation. The control plane also provides a convenient jumping-off point for all the debugging and monitoring interfaces we use. If we want to watch an operation closely, we can jump from the control plane directly into Datadog logs, traces, or metrics scoped to its cluster(s). When a customer reports high latency, we can quickly pull up the memory/CPU profile in Polar Signals for their query pods. When a customer wants a limit bumped for a namespace, we can inspect the namespace and update the config right there (really!). When all the tools you need are right at hand, you feel more connected to your infra, and on-call sucks a lot less. Your browser does not support the video tag.0:00 / 0:00Jump from the control plane to logs, traces, and metrics already scoped to the right context. This dashboard is not just a vibe-coded sidecar to the control plane. We treat it as first-class software and invest engineering effort into it, so the complexity of operating the clusters stays mostly hidden behind a simple, fast, keyboard-driven interface. Fleet operations While the control plane has scaled very well, we started to feel the toil of fleet-wide upgrades: manually selecting clusters and a target SHA, kicking off the upgrade, monitoring it, and making sure things looked ok before proceeding to the rest. The larger our fleet got, the more painful it became to sequence and babysit a rollout that could last hours. Now, any operation can be submitted as a fleet operation, and the control plane's fleet controller will roll it out across a sequence of waves containing one or more clusters. Between waves, a gate checks that every cluster in the wave upgraded successfully and that our monitors are quiet. If a monitor fires or any cluster fails, the fleet controller pauses the rollout and notifies us in Slack, limiting the fallout from a bad deploy. Importantly, nothing changes for the cluster agent. It has no concept of a fleet or fleet operation. It still polls the API server for its pending operations, and its status transitions are still mirrored back into the same MySQL table. Every operation is still the same CRD driven by the same local state machine. Orchestrating 100s of them is effectively just a loop over existing primitives. Simplicity scales turbopuffer's architecture is easy to reason about and easy to be on call for. It would be a shame if it wasn't also easy to deploy to. The design decisions we make in the control plane all funnel toward simplicity: a single control plane for all deployment models, a single CRD for every operation, a single UI to manage the entire fleet. This simplicity has allowed us to scale the control plane from managing just a few public regions to 100+ clusters across dozens of regions and multiple deployment models. We believe its simplicity will allow us to maintain our shipping speed even as we scale to 1000s. turbopufferturbopuffer is a fast search engine that hosts 1T+ documents, handles 10M+ writes/s, and serves 25k+ queries/s. sentences.zh: 一些 BYOC 供应商通过要求客户创建一个专用云帐户并在其中授予供应商常设管理凭据来解决此问题。

sentences.en: That keeps the rest of the customer's cloud account isolated, but every dedicated account creates security monitoring + compliance + billing overhead that we generally prefer to avoid.
sentences.zh: 这使客户的云帐户的其余部分保持隔离，但每个专用帐户都会产生我们通常希望避免的安全监控+合规性+计费开销。

blocks.html_en: We don't want different control planes for BYOC and SaaS, so we have to design for the lowest common denominator. We must be able to operate every cluster without reaching in.

sentences.en: We don't want different control planes for BYOC and SaaS, so we have to design for the lowest common denominator.
sentences.zh: 我们不希望 BYOC 和 SaaS 使用不同的控制平面，因此我们必须针对最低公分母进行设计。

sentences.en: We must be able to operate every cluster without reaching in.
sentences.zh: 我们必须能够在不触及的情况下操作每个集群。

blocks.html_en: How do you operate a database cluster you can't touch?

sentences.en: How do you operate a database cluster you can't touch?
sentences.zh: 触不可及的数据库集群如何运营？

blocks.html_en: The only way this works is if every operation we need to perform on a cluster can run without us reaching in. The cluster must be able to independently drive its operations to a terminal state, even if it loses its connection to the central control plane.

sentences.en: The only way this works is if every operation we need to perform on a cluster can run without us reaching in.
sentences.zh: 唯一可行的方法是，我们需要在集群上执行的每个操作都可以在我们不介入的情况下运行。

sentences.en: The cluster must be able to independently drive its operations to a terminal state, even if it loses its connection to the central control plane.
sentences.zh: 集群必须能够独立地将其操作驱动到最终状态，即使它失去了与中央控制平面的连接。

blocks.html_en: The solution to this is standard Kubernetes stuff. On every cluster, we run a local cluster agent that implements a simple state machine. A single Kubernetes CRD called TurbopufferOperation expresses every operation kind, from upgrade to tidy. A Kubernetes controller drives each custom resource (CR) from state to state via a reconciliation loop until it reaches a terminal state. Operations advance on their own by default, but BYOC customers can gate operations on approval or maintenance windows. These are baked into the CRD as waiting states that advance when approvals are given or the window opens.

sentences.en: The solution to this is standard Kubernetes stuff.
sentences.zh: 解决这个问题的方法是使用标准的 Kubernetes 东西。

sentences.en: On every cluster, we run a local cluster agent that implements a simple state machine.
sentences.zh: 在每个集群上，我们运行一个本地集群代理来实现一个简单的状态机。

sentences.en: A single Kubernetes CRD called TurbopufferOperation expresses every operation kind, from upgrade to tidy.
sentences.zh: 一个名为 TurbopufferOperation 的 Kubernetes CRD 表达了从升级到整理的每种操作类型。

sentences.en: A Kubernetes controller drives each custom resource (CR) from state to state via a reconciliation loop until it reaches a terminal state.
sentences.zh: Kubernetes 控制器通过协调循环将每个自定义资源 (CR) 从一个状态驱动到另一个状态，直到达到最终状态。

sentences.en: Operations advance on their own by default, but BYOC customers can gate operations on approval or maintenance windows.
sentences.zh: 默认情况下，操作会自行推进，但 BYOC 客户可以在审批或维护窗口中控制操作。

sentences.en: These are baked into the CRD as waiting states that advance when approvals are given or the window opens.
sentences.zh: 这些作为等待状态被纳入 CRD 中，当获得批准或窗口打开时，这些等待状态就会提前。

blocks.html_en: The key is to define states that are generic enough to model every operation kind, both existing and future, but finite enough that the reconciler can always drive them toward a terminal state. We never need to reach in to do work, and the state lives as a durable object in the cluster's own etcd. If the agent crashes or loses its connection to the control plane, it can still drive that work to completion.

sentences.en: The key is to define states that are generic enough to model every operation kind, both existing and future, but finite enough that the reconciler can always drive them toward a terminal state.
sentences.zh: 关键是定义足够通用的状态来对每种操作类型（现有的和未来的）进行建模，但又足够有限，以便协调器始终可以将它们推向最终状态。

sentences.en: We never need to reach in to do work, and the state lives as a durable object in the cluster's own etcd.
sentences.zh: 我们永远不需要进行工作，并且状态作为集群自己的 etcd 中的持久对象存在。

sentences.en: If the agent crashes or loses its connection to the control plane, it can still drive that work to completion.
sentences.zh: 如果代理崩溃或失去与控制平面的连接，它仍然可以推动该工作完成。

blocks.html_en: The local, durable state machine means we don't have to reach into a cluster to drive its work, but how does a cluster get its work?

sentences.en: The local, durable state machine means we don't have to reach into a cluster to drive its work, but how does a cluster get its work?
sentences.zh: 本地、持久的状态机意味着我们不必进入集群来驱动其工作，但是集群如何获得其工作呢？

blocks.html_en: You use Terraform, right?

sentences.en: You use Terraform, right?
sentences.zh: 您使用 Terraform，对吧？

blocks.html_en: The default here would be to reach for infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tools like Terraform and Helm. These tools are great for provisioning infrastructure. We use them for that! But they're the wrong control plane for operating a fleet of databases.

sentences.en: The default here would be to reach for infrastructure-as-code (IaC) tools like Terraform and Helm.
sentences.zh: 这里的默认设置是使用 Terraform 和 Helm 等基础设施即代码 (IaC) 工具。

sentences.en: These tools are great for provisioning infrastructure.
sentences.zh: 这些工具非常适合配置基础设施。

sentences.en: We use them for that!
sentences.zh: 我们用它们来实现这个目的！

sentences.en: But they're the wrong control plane for operating a fleet of databases.
sentences.zh: 但它们对于操作数据库群来说是错误的控制平面。

blocks.html_en: First, we do not have a dedicated DevOps function at turbopuffer. We ask our database engineers to deploy their code to the infra. Most of them haven't used IaC tools much in the past, so it doesn't make sense to put those tools in their critical path.

sentences.en: First, we do not have a dedicated DevOps function at turbopuffer.
sentences.zh: 首先，我们在turbopuffer 没有专门的DevOps 功能。

sentences.en: We ask our database engineers to deploy their code to the infra.
sentences.zh: 我们要求我们的数据库工程师将他们的代码部署到基础设施中。

sentences.en: Most of them haven't used IaC tools much in the past, so it doesn't make sense to put those tools in their critical path.
sentences.zh: 他们中的大多数人过去没有太多使用 IaC 工具，因此将这些工具放在关键路径中是没有意义的。

blocks.html_en: Second, Terraform's default model would require us to run terraform apply from our own infrastructure with the customer's infra as the target, which we can't do for BYOC. A GitOps flow for Terraform could solve this by having the customer automatically trigger terraform apply from within their cloud account whenever a Git repo is updated. For database upgrades, this could theoretically work: just bump the Docker image in the Terraform config. But who owns the repo? If it's ours, BYOC customers who want an approval gate have no control over merges. If it's theirs, we're back to needing write access into their systems or waiting on humans to merge the PR.

sentences.en: Second, Terraform's default model would require us to run terraform apply from our own infrastructure with the customer's infra as the target, which we can't do for BYOC.
sentences.zh: 其次，Terraform 的默认模型要求我们从我们自己的基础设施运行 terraform apply，并以客户的基础设施为目标，而对于 BYOC，我们无法做到这一点。

sentences.en: A GitOps flow for Terraform could solve this by having the customer automatically trigger terraform apply from within their cloud account whenever a Git repo is updated.
sentences.zh: Terraform 的 GitOps 流程可以通过让客户在 Git 存储库更新时自动从其云帐户内触发 terraform 应用来解决此问题。

sentences.en: For database upgrades, this could theoretically work: just bump the Docker image in the Terraform config.
sentences.zh: 对于数据库升级，这在理论上是可行的：只需在 Terraform 配置中修改 Docker 镜像即可。

sentences.en: But who owns the repo?
sentences.zh: 但谁拥有该回购协议？

sentences.en: If it's ours, BYOC customers who want an approval gate have no control over merges.
sentences.zh: 如果是我们的，想要批准门的 BYOC 客户无法控制合并。

sentences.en: If it's theirs, we're back to needing write access into their systems or waiting on humans to merge the PR.
sentences.zh: 如果是他们的，我们又需要对他们的系统进行写访问或等待人类合并 PR。

blocks.html_en: Either way, many of our operations have a less declarative shape. Things like one-off namespace reindexing, compacting a WAL, or garbage collecting the LSM are jobs to be done, not states to be arrived at. Every ad hoc operation would need to be a git commit with a new manifest to create the job, then a commit to garbage collect the completed jobs. Terraform files make great declarative manifests, but terrible job queues.

sentences.en: Either way, many of our operations have a less declarative shape.
sentences.zh: 不管怎样，我们的许多运营都没有那么明确。

sentences.en: Things like one-off namespace reindexing, compacting a WAL, or garbage collecting the LSM are jobs to be done, not states to be arrived at.
sentences.zh: 诸如一次性命名空间重新索引、压缩 WAL 或 LSM 垃圾收集之类的事情是需要完成的工作，而不是需要到达的状态。

sentences.en: Every ad hoc operation would need to be a git commit with a new manifest to create the job, then a commit to garbage collect the completed jobs.
sentences.zh: 每个临时操作都需要使用新清单进行 git 提交来创建作业，然后提交对已完成的作业进行垃圾收集。

sentences.en: Terraform files make great declarative manifests, but terrible job queues.
sentences.zh: Terraform 文件具有很好的声明性清单，但工作队列却很糟糕。

blocks.html_en: How the agent fetches work (and how we keep track of it)

sentences.en: How the agent fetches work (and how we keep track of it)
sentences.zh: 代理如何获取工作（以及我们如何跟踪它）

blocks.html_en: We can't reach into a cluster, and we won't use GitOps, but the cluster still needs to be able to pull its work from the control plane and push its status back out. The system must be fully tolerant of a lost connection between cluster and control plane; a control plane outage should not take down an otherwise healthy cluster. In the event of a lost connection, the cluster should be able to pick up its new operations once it reconnects, while the control plane should be able to catch up on the state of the cluster.

sentences.en: We can't reach into a cluster, and we won't use GitOps, but the cluster still needs to be able to pull its work from the control plane and push its status back out.
sentences.zh: 我们无法访问集群，也不会使用 GitOps，但集群仍然需要能够从控制平面拉取其工作并将其状态推回。

sentences.en: The system must be fully tolerant of a lost connection between cluster and control plane; a control plane outage should not take down an otherwise healthy cluster.
sentences.zh: 系统必须完全容忍集群和控制平面之间的连接丢失；控制平面中断不应导致原本健康的集群瘫痪。

sentences.en: In the event of a lost connection, the cluster should be able to pick up its new operations once it reconnects, while the control plane should be able to catch up on the state of the cluster.
sentences.zh: 如果连接丢失，集群应该能够在重新连接后继续执行新操作，而控制平面应该能够赶上集群的状态。

blocks.html_en: To accomplish these aims, we built a custom central control plane consisting of an API server backed by a PlanetScale MySQL database.

sentences.en: To accomplish these aims, we built a custom central control plane consisting of an API server backed by a PlanetScale MySQL database.
sentences.zh: 为了实现这些目标，我们构建了一个自定义中央控制平面，其中包含由 PlanetScale MySQL 数据库支持的 API 服务器。

blocks.html_en: Each cluster agent is given a cluster-specific API key. To fetch its operations, the agent regularly polls the API server via an authenticated GET request, to which the API server responds with that cluster's pending operations. Once the agent gets its operations, it stores them as custom resources and starts running them through its reconciliation loop. This is idempotent: each operation's CR is named with that operation's ID, so if for some reason a later GET returns the same operation again, the agent will just find the existing CR and resume from the state stored in etcd instead of creating a duplicate.

sentences.en: Each cluster agent is given a cluster-specific API key.
sentences.zh: 每个集群代理都会获得一个特定于集群的 API 密钥。

sentences.en: To fetch its operations, the agent regularly polls the API server via an authenticated GET request, to which the API server responds with that cluster's pending operations.
sentences.zh: 为了获取其操作，代理会通过经过身份验证的 GET 请求定期轮询 API 服务器，API 服务器会使用该集群的待处理操作来响应该请求。

sentences.en: Once the agent gets its operations, it stores them as custom resources and starts running them through its reconciliation loop.
sentences.zh: 一旦代理获得其操作，它将它们存储为自定义资源，并开始通过其协调循环运行它们。

sentences.en: This is idempotent: each operation's CR is named with that operation's ID, so if for some reason a later GET returns the same operation again, the agent will just find the existing CR and resume from the state stored in etcd instead of creating a duplicate.
sentences.zh: 这是幂等的：每个操作的 CR 都以该操作的 ID 命名，因此如果由于某种原因稍后的 GET 再次返回相同的操作，代理将只找到现有的 CR 并从存储在 etcd 中的状态恢复，而不是创建副本。

blocks.html_en: As the operations advance, the cluster agent will periodically POST its buffered status transitions back to the API server, which mirrors them into a status_transitions table in MySQL as an append-only log.

sentences.en: As the operations advance, the cluster agent will periodically POST its buffered status transitions back to the API server, which mirrors them into a status_transitions table in MySQL as an append-only log.
sentences.zh: 随着操作的进行，集群代理将定期将其缓冲的状态转换发布回 API 服务器，API 服务器将它们作为仅附加日志镜像到 MySQL 中的 status_transitions 表中。

blocks.html_en: If the agent's POST fails to get a response, the agent puts the transitions back into its buffer and tries again. The POST may have landed even if the response didn't come back, so the same transition could show up twice in the log. That doesn't matter: an operation's current state is just its latest transition.

sentences.en: If the agent's POST fails to get a response, the agent puts the transitions back into its buffer and tries again.
sentences.zh: 如果代理的 POST 未能获得响应，代理会将转换放回到其缓冲区中并重试。

sentences.en: The POST may have landed even if the response didn't come back, so the same transition could show up twice in the log.
sentences.zh: 即使响应没有返回，POST 也可能已到达，因此相同的转换可能会在日志中显示两次。

sentences.en: That doesn't matter: an operation's current state is just its latest transition.
sentences.zh: 这并不重要：操作的当前状态只是其最新的转换。

blocks.html_en: This is how we keep the central control plane in sync with each cluster even in the event of temporary connection loss. The database maintains the source of truth for the desired operations we want to run on every cluster, and holds a mirror of the status of those operations so we can rebuild a cluster's state from afar.

sentences.en: This is how we keep the central control plane in sync with each cluster even in the event of temporary connection loss.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们如何保持中央控制平面与每个集群同步，即使在临时连接丢失的情况下也是如此。

sentences.en: The database maintains the source of truth for the desired operations we want to run on every cluster, and holds a mirror of the status of those operations so we can rebuild a cluster's state from afar.
sentences.zh: 数据库维护我们想要在每个集群上运行的所需操作的真实来源，并保存这些操作状态的镜像，以便我们可以远程重建集群的状态。

blocks.html_en: But a database is a dangerous interface. We said we didn't want to ship code with YAML — it would be insane to replace that with INSERT INTO SQL statements.

sentences.en: But a database is a dangerous interface.
sentences.zh: 但数据库是一个危险的接口。

sentences.en: We said we didn't want to ship code with YAML — it would be insane to replace that with INSERT INTO SQL statements.
sentences.zh: 我们说过我们不想用 YAML 来发布代码——用 INSERT INTO SQL 语句替换它是疯狂的。

blocks.html_en: An interface we actually like using

sentences.en: An interface we actually like using
sentences.zh: 我们真正喜欢使用的界面

blocks.html_en: We deploy every day, multiple times per day, and debug and maintain the clusters in between deploys. If you're a turbopuffer database engineer, you want the control plane to be as reliable and easy to use as your favorite code editor.

sentences.en: We deploy every day, multiple times per day, and debug and maintain the clusters in between deploys.
sentences.zh: 我们每天都会部署多次，并在部署之间调试和维护集群。

sentences.en: If you're a turbopuffer database engineer, you want the control plane to be as reliable and easy to use as your favorite code editor.
sentences.zh: 如果您是一名 TurboPuffer 数据库工程师，您希望控制平面像您最喜欢的代码编辑器一样可靠且易于使用。

blocks.html_en: The control plane has a custom Remix/React dashboard that fronts the API server. The UX is inspired by Linear: everything has a hotkey, so you can operate it entirely from the keyboard. The information hierarchy is structured, and the selection state is clear, so you know exactly which clusters you're working on.

sentences.en: The control plane has a custom Remix/React dashboard that fronts the API server.
sentences.zh: 控制平面有一个位于 API 服务器前面的自定义 Remix/React 仪表板。

sentences.en: The UX is inspired by Linear: everything has a hotkey, so you can operate it entirely from the keyboard.
sentences.zh: UX 的灵感来自 Linear：一切都有热键，因此您可以完全通过键盘进行操作。

sentences.en: The information hierarchy is structured, and the selection state is clear, so you know exactly which clusters you're working on.
sentences.zh: 信息层次结构清晰，选择状态清晰，因此您可以准确地知道正在处理哪些集群。

blocks.html_en: Upgrades are the most common operation, and the UI reflects that. We can quickly see each cluster's deployed commit SHA and how far it has drifted from the latest passing SHA, with metadata pulled from GitHub (commit message, PR number, commit date) so we don't have to decipher the SHA. Upgrades are typically done in groups, so we can select multiple clusters across all deployment models, choose a target commit SHA, and upgrade all of them from the keyboard. We can similarly kick off all other operations from this UI.

sentences.en: Upgrades are the most common operation, and the UI reflects that.
sentences.zh: 升级是最常见的操作，UI 也反映了这一点。

sentences.en: We can quickly see each cluster's deployed commit SHA and how far it has drifted from the latest passing SHA, with metadata pulled from GitHub (commit message, PR number, commit date) so we don't have to decipher the SHA.
sentences.zh: 我们可以快速查看每个集群部署的提交 SHA 以及它与最新通过的 SHA 的偏差程度，并使用从 GitHub 提取的元数据（提交消息、PR 编号、提交日期），因此我们无需破译 SHA。

sentences.en: Upgrades are typically done in groups, so we can select multiple clusters across all deployment models, choose a target commit SHA, and upgrade all of them from the keyboard.
sentences.zh: 升级通常是分组完成的，因此我们可以在所有部署模型中选择多个集群，选择目标提交 SHA，然后通过键盘升级所有集群。

sentences.en: We can similarly kick off all other operations from this UI.
sentences.zh: 我们可以类似地从此 UI 启动所有其他操作。

blocks.html_en: <figcaption>Select clusters, pick a target SHA, and roll out upgrades from the keyboard.</figcaption>

sentences.en: Select clusters, pick a target SHA, and roll out upgrades from the keyboard.
sentences.zh: 选择集群，选择目标 SHA，然后通过键盘进行升级。

blocks.html_en: We don't expect our engineers to be in the dashboard all the time, so we stream status transitions for each operation into a dedicated Slack thread. If an operation fails, it fails loudly into the channel for people to react to and fix. This gets our attention without us having to babysit.

sentences.en: We don't expect our engineers to be in the dashboard all the time, so we stream status transitions for each operation into a dedicated Slack thread.
sentences.zh: 我们不希望工程师一直在仪表板中，因此我们将每个操作的状态转换流式传输到专用的 Slack 线程中。

sentences.en: If an operation fails, it fails loudly into the channel for people to react to and fix.
sentences.zh: 如果一个操作失败了，它就会大声地进入失败频道，供人们做出反应并修复。

sentences.en: This gets our attention without us having to babysit.
sentences.zh: 这引起了我们的注意，而无需我们照顾。

blocks.html_en: When an approval is needed for operations on a BYOC cluster, the same Slack integration automatically notifies the customer through their dedicated Slack support channel so they can approve.

sentences.en: When an approval is needed for operations on a BYOC cluster, the same Slack integration automatically notifies the customer through their dedicated Slack support channel so they can approve.
sentences.zh: 当 BYOC 集群上的操作需要批准时，相同的 Slack 集成会自动通过客户的专用 Slack 支持渠道通知客户，以便他们进行批准。

blocks.html_en: <figcaption>Upgrade threads show commit diffs, rollout status, and the conversation around the operation.</figcaption>

sentences.en: Upgrade threads show commit diffs, rollout status, and the conversation around the operation.
sentences.zh: 升级线程显示提交差异、部署状态以及围绕操作的对话。

blocks.html_en: The control plane also provides a convenient jumping-off point for all the debugging and monitoring interfaces we use. If we want to watch an operation closely, we can jump from the control plane directly into Datadog logs, traces, or metrics scoped to its cluster(s). When a customer reports high latency, we can quickly pull up the memory/CPU profile in Polar Signals for their query pods. When a customer wants a limit bumped for a namespace, we can inspect the namespace and update the config right there (really!). When all the tools you need are right at hand, you feel more connected to your infra, and on-call sucks a lot less.

sentences.en: The control plane also provides a convenient jumping-off point for all the debugging and monitoring interfaces we use.
sentences.zh: 控制平面还为我们使用的所有调试和监控接口提供了一个方便的起点。

sentences.en: If we want to watch an operation closely, we can jump from the control plane directly into Datadog logs, traces, or metrics scoped to its cluster(s).
sentences.zh: 如果我们想密切观察操作，我们可以从控制平面直接跳转到 Datadog 日志、跟踪或集群范围内的指标。

sentences.en: When a customer reports high latency, we can quickly pull up the memory/CPU profile in Polar Signals for their query pods.
sentences.zh: 当客户报告高延迟时，我们可以快速在 Polar Signals 中提取其查询 Pod 的内存/CPU 配置文件。

sentences.en: When a customer wants a limit bumped for a namespace, we can inspect the namespace and update the config right there (really!).
sentences.zh: 当客户希望提高命名空间的限制时，我们可以检查命名空间并立即更新配置（真的！）。

sentences.en: When all the tools you need are right at hand, you feel more connected to your infra, and on-call sucks a lot less.
sentences.zh: 当您需要的所有工具都在手边时，您会感觉与基础设施的联系更加紧密，并且随叫随到的麻烦也少了很多。

blocks.html_en: <figcaption>Jump from the control plane to logs, traces, and metrics already scoped to the right context.</figcaption>

sentences.en: Jump from the control plane to logs, traces, and metrics already scoped to the right context.
sentences.zh: 从控制平面跳转到已经限定在正确上下文范围内的日志、跟踪和指标。

BYOC 的问题

BYOC 集群位于客户的云帐户内，默认情况下我们不持有该帐户的凭据。 我们不能只通过 SSH 或 kubectl 进入。 一些 BYOC 供应商通过要求客户创建一个专用云帐户并在其中授予供应商常设管理凭据来解决此问题。 这使客户的云帐户的其余部分保持隔离，但每个专用帐户都会产生我们通常希望避免的安全监控+合规性+计费开销。

我们不希望 BYOC 和 SaaS 使用不同的控制平面，因此我们必须针对最低公分母进行设计。 我们必须能够在不触及的情况下操作每个集群。

触不可及的数据库集群如何运营？

唯一可行的方法是，我们需要在集群上执行的每个操作都可以在我们不介入的情况下运行。 集群必须能够独立地将其操作驱动到最终状态，即使它失去了与中央控制平面的连接。

解决这个问题的方法是使用标准的 Kubernetes 东西。 在每个集群上，我们运行一个本地集群代理来实现一个简单的状态机。 一个名为 TurbopufferOperation 的 Kubernetes CRD 表达了从升级到整理的每种操作类型。 Kubernetes 控制器通过协调循环将每个自定义资源 (CR) 从一个状态驱动到另一个状态，直到达到最终状态。 默认情况下，操作会自行推进，但 BYOC 客户可以在审批或维护窗口中控制操作。 这些作为等待状态被纳入 CRD 中，当获得批准或窗口打开时，这些等待状态就会提前。

关键是定义足够通用的状态来对每种操作类型（现有的和未来的）进行建模，但又足够有限，以便协调器始终可以将它们推向最终状态。 我们永远不需要进行工作，并且状态作为集群自己的 etcd 中的持久对象存在。 如果代理崩溃或失去与控制平面的连接，它仍然可以推动该工作完成。

本地、持久的状态机意味着我们不必进入集群来驱动其工作，但是集群如何获得其工作呢？

您使用 Terraform，对吧？

这里的默认设置是使用 Terraform 和 Helm 等基础设施即代码 (IaC) 工具。 这些工具非常适合配置基础设施。 我们用它们来实现这个目的！ 但它们对于操作数据库群来说是错误的控制平面。

首先，我们在turbopuffer 没有专门的DevOps 功能。 我们要求我们的数据库工程师将他们的代码部署到基础设施中。 他们中的大多数人过去没有太多使用 IaC 工具，因此将这些工具放在关键路径中是没有意义的。

其次，Terraform 的默认模型要求我们从我们自己的基础设施运行 terraform apply，并以客户的基础设施为目标，而对于 BYOC，我们无法做到这一点。 Terraform 的 GitOps 流程可以通过让客户在 Git 存储库更新时自动从其云帐户内触发 terraform 应用来解决此问题。 对于数据库升级，这在理论上是可行的：只需在 Terraform 配置中修改 Docker 镜像即可。 但谁拥有该回购协议？ 如果是我们的，想要批准门的 BYOC 客户无法控制合并。 如果是他们的，我们又需要对他们的系统进行写访问或等待人类合并 PR。

不管怎样，我们的许多运营都没有那么明确。 诸如一次性命名空间重新索引、压缩 WAL 或 LSM 垃圾收集之类的事情是需要完成的工作，而不是需要到达的状态。 每个临时操作都需要使用新清单进行 git 提交来创建作业，然后提交对已完成的作业进行垃圾收集。 Terraform 文件具有很好的声明性清单，但工作队列却很糟糕。

代理如何获取工作（以及我们如何跟踪它）

我们无法访问集群，也不会使用 GitOps，但集群仍然需要能够从控制平面拉取其工作并将其状态推回。 系统必须完全容忍集群和控制平面之间的连接丢失；控制平面中断不应导致原本健康的集群瘫痪。 如果连接丢失，集群应该能够在重新连接后继续执行新操作，而控制平面应该能够赶上集群的状态。

为了实现这些目标，我们构建了一个自定义中央控制平面，其中包含由 PlanetScale MySQL 数据库支持的 API 服务器。

每个集群代理都会获得一个特定于集群的 API 密钥。 为了获取其操作，代理会通过经过身份验证的 GET 请求定期轮询 API 服务器，API 服务器会使用该集群的待处理操作来响应该请求。 一旦代理获得其操作，它将它们存储为自定义资源，并开始通过其协调循环运行它们。 这是幂等的：每个操作的 CR 都以该操作的 ID 命名，因此如果由于某种原因稍后的 GET 再次返回相同的操作，代理将只找到现有的 CR 并从存储在 etcd 中的状态恢复，而不是创建副本。

随着操作的进行，集群代理将定期将其缓冲的状态转换发布回 API 服务器，API 服务器将它们作为仅附加日志镜像到 MySQL 中的 status_transitions 表中。

如果代理的 POST 未能获得响应，代理会将转换放回到其缓冲区中并重试。 即使响应没有返回，POST 也可能已到达，因此相同的转换可能会在日志中显示两次。 这并不重要：操作的当前状态只是其最新的转换。

这就是我们如何保持中央控制平面与每个集群同步，即使在临时连接丢失的情况下也是如此。 数据库维护我们想要在每个集群上运行的所需操作的真实来源，并保存这些操作状态的镜像，以便我们可以远程重建集群的状态。

但数据库是一个危险的接口。 我们说过我们不想用 YAML 来发布代码——用 INSERT INTO SQL 语句替换它是疯狂的。

我们真正喜欢使用的界面

我们每天都会部署多次，并在部署之间调试和维护集群。 如果您是一名 TurboPuffer 数据库工程师，您希望控制平面像您最喜欢的代码编辑器一样可靠且易于使用。

控制平面有一个位于 API 服务器前面的自定义 Remix/React 仪表板。 UX 的灵感来自 Linear：一切都有热键，因此您可以完全通过键盘进行操作。 信息层次结构清晰，选择状态清晰，因此您可以准确地知道正在处理哪些集群。

升级是最常见的操作，UI 也反映了这一点。 我们可以快速查看每个集群部署的提交 SHA 以及它与最新通过的 SHA 的偏差程度，并使用从 GitHub 提取的元数据（提交消息、PR 编号、提交日期），因此我们无需破译 SHA。 升级通常是分组完成的，因此我们可以在所有部署模型中选择多个集群，选择目标提交 SHA，然后通过键盘升级所有集群。 我们可以类似地从此 UI 启动所有其他操作。

我们不希望工程师一直在仪表板中，因此我们将每个操作的状态转换流式传输到专用的 Slack 线程中。 如果一个操作失败了，它就会大声地进入失败频道，供人们做出反应并修复。 这引起了我们的注意，而无需我们照顾。

当 BYOC 集群上的操作需要批准时，相同的 Slack 集成会自动通过客户的专用 Slack 支持渠道通知客户，以便他们进行批准。

控制平面还为我们使用的所有调试和监控接口提供了一个方便的起点。 如果我们想密切观察操作，我们可以从控制平面直接跳转到 Datadog 日志、跟踪或集群范围内的指标。 当客户报告高延迟时，我们可以快速在 Polar Signals 中提取其查询 Pod 的内存/CPU 配置文件。 当客户希望提高命名空间的限制时，我们可以检查命名空间并立即更新配置（真的！）。 当您需要的所有工具都在手边时，您会感觉与基础设施的联系更加紧密，并且随叫随到的麻烦也少了很多。

该仪表板不仅仅是控制平面的振动编码边车。 我们将其视为一流的软件，并对其进行了工程投入，因此操作集群的复杂性大部分隐藏在简单、快速、键盘驱动的界面后面。

车队运营

虽然控制平面的扩展性非常好，但我们开始感受到整个机群升级的艰辛：手动选择集群和目标 SHA、启动升级、监控升级并确保一切正常，然后再进行其余操作。 我们的机队规模越大，对可能持续数小时的部署进行排序和照管就变得越痛苦。

现在，任何操作都可以作为舰队操作提交，并且控制平面的舰队控制器将在包含一个或多个集群的一系列波中展开该操作。 在 Wave 之间，一个门会检查 Wave 中的每个集群是否已成功升级，以及我们的监视器是否安静。 如果监视器发生故障或任何集群发生故障，队列控制器会暂停部署并在 Slack 中通知我们，从而限制部署不当造成的后果。

重要的是，集群代理没有任何变化。 它没有舰队或舰队运营的概念。 它仍然轮询 API 服务器以查找其挂起的操作，并且其状态转换仍然镜像回同一个 MySQL 表中。 每个操作仍然是由相同的本地状态机驱动的相同的 CRD。 编排其中的数百个实际上只是现有原语的循环。

简单尺度

turbopuffer 的架构很容易推理，也很容易随叫随到。 如果它不容易部署，那将是一种耻辱。 我们在控制平面中做出的设计决策都趋向于简单性：用于所有部署模型的单个控制平面、用于每个操作的单个 CRD、用于管理整个队列的单个 UI。

这种简单性使我们能够将控制平面从仅管理几个公共区域扩展到跨数十个区域和多种部署模型的 100 多个集群。 我们相信，即使我们的规模扩大到 1000 台，它的简单性也将使我们能够保持我们的运输速度。
